bodyHtml:
Does a root canal hurt?

For most people, a root canal today feels a lot like having a routine filling: with modern local anaesthetic, you can expect little to no pain during the procedure itself, and usually only mild soreness for a few days afterward as the area settles. The reputation root canals carry for being agonising comes largely from the past and from the toothache that often sends people to the dentist in the first place — not from the treatment as it is practised now. No dentist can honestly promise a completely painless experience for every single person, but genuine comfort during treatment is now the norm rather than the exception.

Why people expect pain — and why that picture is dated

A great deal of the fear comes from stories passed down from decades ago, before today's anaesthetics, instruments, and techniques were common. It is also worth remembering that the severe pain many people associate with needing a root canal is usually caused by the infected or inflamed nerve before any treatment begins. In that sense, a root canal is designed to relieve pain, not create it. Once the inflamed pulp tissue is removed and the tooth is cleaned, the source of that throbbing ache is addressed.

What you actually feel during treatment

The first step is numbing the area with local anaesthetic. You may feel a brief pinch or pressure as the freezing is placed, and then the tooth and surrounding tissues go numb. During the procedure you will typically feel pressure, vibration, and movement — sensations rather than sharp pain. Many people are surprised by how uneventful it is, and some even doze off. If you do feel anything sharp, you can raise your hand and let the dental team know; they can add more anaesthetic. Telling your dentist about any discomfort as it happens is one of the most useful things you can do for your own comfort.

What about afterward?

Once the freezing wears off, it is common to have some tenderness around the tooth for a few days, especially when biting. This usually responds well to over-the-counter pain relief and tends to improve steadily. Most people are back to their normal routine quickly. Soreness that is severe, worsening, or accompanied by swelling is less typical and worth a call to your dentist.

Things that make treatment more comfortable

  • Treating sooner rather than later. A tooth with active, acute infection can sometimes be harder to numb fully, so addressing problems early often makes for a smoother visit.
  • Speaking up. Letting your dentist know you are nervous, or that you felt something, lets them adjust.
  • Asking about options. If anxiety is a major barrier, it is reasonable to ask a clinic what comfort measures they offer.

Why was my tooth so painful before treatment?

Pulp inflammation and infection can cause intense, lingering pain because the nerve inside the tooth is sensitive and enclosed in a rigid space with nowhere for pressure to go. This is the pain that treatment is meant to resolve — which is why many people feel relief in the days after a root canal, once healing is underway.

Is a root canal more painful than an extraction?

Both procedures are done with the area numbed, and both involve some aftercare. Many people assume pulling a tooth is the simpler or less uncomfortable route, but removing a tooth also involves healing and the separate question of how to replace it. Which option is appropriate depends on your particular tooth, and your dentist can walk you through the trade-offs.

Will I be able to feel the tooth during the root canal?

You should not feel pain once the area is properly frozen. Pressure and vibration are normal and expected. If sharp sensation breaks through, that is a signal to pause and add more anaesthetic rather than to push through.

A measured, comfortable approach

If worry about pain has been keeping you from dealing with a troublesome tooth, it may help to talk through the process with a dentist before anything is decided. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, provides root canal treatment at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, where you can ask questions and understand your options before treatment begins. You can also read more about root canal therapy at the Markham clinic to learn what the process involves.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
